sections.h2: How do you sell a house fast in Camden, NJ?
sections.html:
In Camden the quickest sale is a cash purchase from a buyer who accepts the house as it is and handles the city's sale certificate. A listing can work for houses in good shape in neighborhoods with active demand, but the city's resale rules add steps whichever way you go. Selling yourself without an agent is allowed, with the same paperwork.

Camden is the Camden County seat on the Delaware River, directly across from Philadelphia. The Census Bureau estimates 71,430 residents on July 1, 2025, a 0.5% dip from the 2020 base, down from 77,344 at the 2010 Census. It covers 8.92 square miles of land and 1.42 square miles of water, with a 2020 density of about 8,047 people per square mile.

sections.h2: What are Camden homes worth, and who owns them?
sections.html:
Camden values sit far below the rest of the Philadelphia area. Census figures for 2020 to 2024 give a median owner-occupied value of $112,000, median gross rent of $1,226, and just 34.4% of the city's 24,443 households as owners. Median household income is $40,546 and 30.2% of residents are in poverty, so many sellers are carrying a house they cannot afford to repair, or an heir inheriting one.

The most common housing type is the rowhouse, much like Philadelphia's. Yorkship Village, now called Fairview, was the nation's first federally funded planned community for working-class residents. The city recognizes more than 20 neighborhoods, including Cooper Grant, Cramer Hill, East Camden, Parkside, Waterfront South, Rosedale, Pyne Point and Gateway.

  • Rowhouses share walls and roofs, so a buyer's inspection will look closely at party walls and roof drainage.
  • Vacant or fire-damaged houses can still sell, but the buyer may sign an agreement not to occupy until permits are closed.
  • Homes near the waterfront, the Rutgers campus and the hospital district are close to the city's largest employers.

sections.h2: What drives Camden's economy and buyer demand?
sections.html:
About 45% of local employment is in education and medicine, often called "eds and meds." Major employers include Cooper University Hospital, Rutgers University-Camden, Our Lady of Lourdes Medical Center, Campbell's, the Delaware River Port Authority, L3Harris, the State of New Jersey and Subaru of America, which moved its headquarters here from Pennsauken in 2018. The Port of Camden handles wood products, cocoa and other cargo, and the Philadelphia 76ers training complex sits on the waterfront near the Adventure Aquarium, the Battleship New Jersey and the Freedom Mortgage Pavilion.

In October 2025, the state's Economic Development Authority invited proposals for 16 acres on the North Camden waterfront at the former prison site. Projects like that move buyer attention to nearby streets, but they do not change what your own house is worth, so get a fresh comparison before you decide.

sections.h2: How do schools and transit shape Camden home sales?
sections.html:
Camden City School District runs 19 schools and had 7,553 students in 2020-21, with Camden High, Eastside High, Brimm Medical Arts High, Creative Arts Academy and others serving high school grades. It is one of the former Abbott districts for which the state pays school construction costs. Charter and renaissance schools operate alongside the district, which buyers with children will ask about.

Transit is a real selling point. The PATCO Speedline runs 24 hours to Philadelphia and to Collingswood, Haddonfield, Cherry Hill and Lindenwold, and NJ Transit's River Line light rail runs from Camden to Trenton with four stops in the city. The Walter Rand Transportation Center at Martin Luther King Boulevard and Broadway joins PATCO, River Line and NJ Transit buses. By road, Interstate 676 and U.S. 30 lead to the Benjamin Franklin Bridge, Interstate 76 crosses briefly, and Route 168 touches the south. Mean travel time to work is 23.8 minutes.

sections.h2: What certificate does Camden require before a house is sold?
sections.html:
Camden requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy (the city's building bureau also calls it a Camden Resale Occupancy Certificate) to be applied for and issued before any property in the city is sold or conveyed. The seller is responsible for applying, though the buyer may apply with the seller's written permission. The certificate is issued to the buyer, not the seller. If a buyer closes without one, the buyer stays liable for penalties of up to $2,000 until it issues.

The process starts with a zoning permit at City Hall, then an application to the Construction and Building Bureau, followed by four inspections: building, plumbing, electric and fire. All open building permits must be closed first. If the house is not habitable, the buyer can sign an Agreement to Not Occupy and commit to pulling permits and doing the work. Plan submissions are digital only. A change of tenant in a rental is a different step and goes through the Housing Department.

sections.h2: What rules apply to Camden rental properties?
sections.html:
Camden's Bureau of Housing enforces the city's property maintenance code. Rental properties must be inspected at a change of ownership or occupancy and hold a Rental Approval Certificate before anyone moves in, and buildings with three or more units need a license. To schedule an inspection, all taxes must be current, utilities must be on, the fee is paid when scheduling, and the property must be registered with both the Rent Control office and the Municipal Clerk.

The city has had a rent control ordinance since March 12, 1981. At lease expiration a landlord may raise rent by no more than the lower of the 12-month average consumer price index for the Philadelphia area or 6% of the latest rent, and rent cannot rise during a lease. A buyer of a rental building takes on those limits, so a landlord selling should have the registration file ready.

sections.h2: How do taxes and state fees work when selling in Camden?
sections.html:
Camden's Office of Assessments maintains the tax map, processes senior and veteran deductions and exemptions, receives abatement requests, and handles assessment appeals filed with the Camden County Board of Taxation or the New Jersey Tax Court. The office is in City Hall, Room 329, at 520 Market Street. Check that taxes are current before listing, since the city requires current taxes to schedule a rental inspection and a lien can hold up a closing.

New Jersey's Realty Transfer Fee falls on the seller. At Camden-level prices below $350,000, the schedule is $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 per $500 above that. Senior citizens, blind or disabled sellers and certain low and moderate income housing sales qualify for lower rates, starting at $0.50 per $500 on the first $150,000. The Division of Taxation lists the rates and exemptions.

faqs.q: Who applies for the Certificate of Continued Occupancy in Camden?
faqs.a: The seller. The buyer may file as the seller's agent with written permission, but the certificate is issued to the buyer. The application costs $200 plus a separate $64 fire safety fee.

faqs.q: How long is a Camden occupancy certificate application good for?
faqs.a: Six months. After that a new application must be filed and paid for, unless there are open permits on the property.

faqs.q: Can I sell a vacant or damaged house in Camden?
faqs.a: Yes. If the house is not habitable, the buyer can sign an Agreement to Not Occupy and then obtain permits, do the work and apply for the certificate. Open permits have to be closed before a certificate issues.

faqs.q: Is there rent control in Camden?
faqs.a: Yes. Camden has had a rent control ordinance since 1981, with a cap at the lower of the Philadelphia-area consumer price index or 6% at lease expiration, and landlords register each rental unit annually for $25.

faqs.q: Where do I appeal a Camden property assessment?
faqs.a: Appeals go to the Camden County Board of Taxation or the New Jersey Tax Court. The city's Office of Assessments, at 520 Market Street, Room 329, can explain the process and handles deductions.
